speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head P of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our threat environment is more complex than it has ever been.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The pace of change is accelerating and hostile actors are quick to exploit new technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is important that Singapore anticipate threats early and invest in capabilities early on to address these threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I focus on four areas which feature heavily in Singapore’s domestic threat landscape; namely, terrorism, cyberattacks, drugs and scams, and look forward to hearing the Ministry’s plans on all these fronts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Globally, terrorist groups continue to incite violence while ongoing conflicts, including those in the Middle East, can inflame sentiments and be exploited by extremists.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore’s international profile and our multicultural society make us an attractive target.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A worrying trend is that of self-radicalisation, which is accelerated by the online environment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The ISD also notes that the timeline from exposure to radicalisation can be as short as weeks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We should pay particular attention to youth radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Youths are particularly vulnerable to radicalisation as they tend to be digital natives, more easily swayed by emotive narratives and are more susceptible to influence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most recently, in November 2025, a 14-year-old Secondary 3 student who was self-radicalised online was issued with a Restriction Order under the ISA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Technology is emerging as an enabler for radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Social media and artificial intelligence (AI) can generate and translate propaganda, produce convincing synthetic media, scale personalised recruitment and even assist in attack planning.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The ISD notes that a 17-year-old ISIS supporter detained in September 2024 used an AI chatbot to generate a "bai’ah", an oath of allegiance, to ISIS, and a declaration of armed jihad against non-Muslims to inspire other Muslims in Singapore to engage in armed violence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In another example, a 17-year-old far-right extremist supporter used an AI chatbot to look for instructions on the production of ammunition and considered producing his own firearms for his local attack plans using three-dimensional printing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the recent case in November 2025, the ISD noted that family members and schoolmates were aware of the youth’s extremist views and tried to dissuade him, but they did not report him to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is a lesson to be learned here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We should continue to educate the public and instil messages that the early reporting is protective, not punitive, and can prevent tragedy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, apart from enforcement, our counter-terrorism efforts must include strong community partnerships, digital literacy and early upstream intervention.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Cyberattacks continue to be a threat to countries worldwide and Singapore is no exception.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They are a national security issue because they can disrupt essential services, compromise sensitive information and erode trust in digital systems which Singapore relies on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the latest Singapore Cyber Landscape report, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) noted a significant increase in cyber attacks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ransomware cases reported to the CSA increased from 132 in 2023 to 159 in 2024, an increase of 21%.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Such cyberattacks can halt operations, especially for organisations which have vulnerable systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As Singapore digitalises further – from healthcare to transport to financial services – the potential impact of a successful attack grows exponentially.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our response must therefore include hardening critical infrastructure, investing in threat detection and strengthening incident response capabilities across agencies and sectors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While Singapore's overall drug situation is under control, drugs continue to be a threat to Singapore's stability.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, new drug abusers increased by 17% to 1,165 in 2025.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of the 1,165 new drug abusers arrested in 2025, half were below 30 years old.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: New drug abusers arrested below 30 years old and 20 years old increased by 9% and 22% respectively in 2025.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In addition, thousands have been caught for possession or use of e-vaporisers since enhanced enforcement began in 2025.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In many cases, what may appear to youths as a lifestyle product has become a gateway to drug abuse, exposing them to serious health risks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This suggests two worrying trends: first, the supply of illegal drugs remains persistent; and second, demand for illegal drugs is increasingly coming from youths.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The convergence of drug abuse with lifestyle trends and online distribution channels means that it is critical that Singapore keeps up its efforts in preventive education, early intervention and strong enforcement against suppliers and traffickers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is perhaps the threat which is felt most closely by Singaporeans today.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The situation remains serious, including a sharp increase in certain types of scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The number of cases and scale of losses show that this is a threat which requires coordinated action across government agencies, banks, telecommunications companies (telcos) and digital platforms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think taking out the hands and legs for scammers in Singapore will go a long way to fighting this scourge, similar to how we took action against loan shark runners and facilitators to battle that scourge.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, whether the threat comes from terrorism, cyberattacks, drugs or scams, our response must be anticipatory and grounded in strong partnerships between the Home Team and other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I look forward to hearing from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) on these matters.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Behind these statistics are individuals struggling with challenges we may not be adequately addressing.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: MHA has recognised that repeat drug abusers face significant barriers: the lack of prosocial networks due to being in and out of the system and difficulty in maintaining employment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Yet what remains insufficiently examined is the mental health dimension underlying these challenges.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This suggests that for individuals cycling in and out of the system, losing jobs and lacking stable support networks, the psychological toll can be devastating, potentially driving them back to the very substance we are trying to help them avoid.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: If so, will this data be made available to researchers or policymakers to better inform our rehabilitation strategies?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Beyond data collection, I urge the Government to strengthen community partnerships that specifically addresses mental health alongside addiction.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Every recovering individual should have ready access to integrated support to help them with underlying mental health conditions that may have contributed to their drug use.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Without this, we are releasing individuals who have served their time in the DRC, facing the same psychological struggles that led them to drugs initially.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Let us build on this momentum by ensuring our approach includes mental health data and integrated support services to help more individuals break free from addiction for good.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I want to speak today not just about policy, but about people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Because behind every label of "ex-offender" is someone's son, someone's spouse, someone's parent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many have made serious mistakes and they have paid dearly for them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But when they step out of prison, they often face a second sentence – rejection, stigma and doors that never open, no matter how hard they try to change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is why we must continue to invest in the 3Rs, or what I call rehabilitation, raising employability and reintegration back into families and the community, not just to reduce reoffending, but to restore dignity, purpose and hope.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When someone is able to work honestly, support their family and belong again, the entire community becomes safer and stronger.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I want to acknowledge the efforts of Yellow Ribbon Singapore and the Singapore Prison Service, and the many employers, voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) and volunteers who lean forward to help.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In our dialogues with employers and ex-offenders, we heard both hope and deep anxiety – hope that employers are willing to give second chances, but fear from those inside that their past will forever define their future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second chances are not about being soft on crime.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are about being firm in our belief that people can change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And when we allow that change to take root, we do not just transform one life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We strengthen families, restore hope and build a more compassionate and resilient Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, this year marks the 50th anniversary of Yellow Ribbon Singapore, formerly SCORE.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Over five decades, the Yellow Ribbon movement has fundamentally reshaped Singapore's approach towards ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It has shifted mindsets from stigma to second chances, mobilised employers across sectors and supported thousands of individuals in rebuilding their lives with dignity and purpose.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It reflects a long-term whole-of-society effort – one that balances accountability with redemption and public safety with social reintegration.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, as with all mature systems, we must continuously review and strengthen what we have built.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: These disruptions would have disproportionately affected individuals attempting to reintegrate into society.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Even so, the figures remind us that reintegration is not automatic.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It is a process that requires sustained support, particularly in the first few years after release.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I therefore support MHA's strengthening of structured aftercare, employer partnerships and skill upgrading pathways.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Employment remains one of the strongest protective factors against reoffending.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But beyond job placement, what matters is job retention and progression.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Stable work builds routine, income stability and self-worth.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: What matters is not simply giving someone a job, but giving them a future.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Where family bonds are intact, the likelihood of successful reintegration increases significantly.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Continued coordination between correctional services, social service agencies and community partners is therefore essential to ensure that counselling, housing stability and financial planning support are aligned rather than fragmented.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: As Yellow Ribbon Singapore turns 50, this milestone offers not only an opportunity to celebrate, but also to consolidate and refine our strategy for the next decade.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, I would also like to speak about scams, which remain a significant societal challenge.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Individuals with weaker financial literacy, unstable employment or limited social support networks may be especially vulnerable, both as victims and, in some cases, as unwitting accomplices such as money mules.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In today's digital economy, financial and cyber awareness are no longer optional competencies.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Encouragingly, the integration of rehabilitation, community partnerships and law enforcement reflects a holistic philosophy – public safety is best protected not only through deterrence, but through prevention and resilience building.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's approach to corrections has long emphasised transformation rather than warehousing.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The Yellow Ribbon movement has demonstrated that when society chooses inclusion over exclusion, many individuals respond positively and rebuild their lives.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: As we commemorate 50 years of Yellow Ribbon Singapore, we should reaffirm three principles.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Second, reintegration must be sustained, extending beyond release into stable employment, family support and community belonging.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Third, vulnerability to emerging risks, including digital scams, must be proactively addressed as part of modern rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I therefore express my support for MHA's ongoing efforts and I am confident that with continued refinement, cross-agency coordination and community partnership, the next chapter of Yellow Ribbon Singapore will be defined not only by compassion, but by measurable progress and enduring impact.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I wish to raise three topics regarding scams – regional cooperation, the impact of the Online Criminal Harms Act (OCHA) and scam victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many online scams targeting Singaporeans are perpetuated overseas and scam compounds housing scammers have been found in some ASEAN countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is thus necessary for agencies across the region to work collaboratively, to share information, conduct operations and extradite suspects where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is the Ministry's assessment of regional cooperation thus far and are there particular obstacles on this front?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Among ASEAN countries, which jurisdictions have not yet joined FRONTIER+ and what are the impediments?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Turning to the domestic scam situation, the mid-year crime brief by the Police in August last year painted a mixed picture.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Those scams and losses in the first half of 2025 decreased from the corresponding period in 2024.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Social media platforms have been an important channel through which scams are perpetuated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is thus disturbing to read of the profits that social media companies have been made from scam ads.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This estimate was based on Meta's own internal documents, which Meta later said were overestimates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has been working with social media companies to put in place anti-scam measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Various directives have been issued to them under the OCHA, to implement measures, such as identity verification and facial recognition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: OCHA has been enforced for nearly two years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is the Ministry's assessment of its effectiveness in preventing scams?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the Government satisfied with the levels of compliance with these directives by social media companies?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is growing research on the psychological impacts of scams on victims being severe, leading to distress, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and even suicidality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Police have stated that there are victim care officers (VCOs) who may be deployed to support victims of crimes, including in scam cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These VCOs are volunteers who need to have relevant background, such as in psychology, social work or counselling.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, scams today no longer are just isolated incidents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They have become organised, industrialised and highly adaptive.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Criminal syndicates test scripts like marketers and A/B-test messages like salespeople and exploit the speed of online platforms to scale harm quickly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They do not wait for trust to be built over years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They manufacture it in minutes through impersonation, fake endorsements, doctored screenshots and increasingly, AI-generated content.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Victims often feel ashamed, families get strained and confidence in institutions can get a hit, especially when scams impersonate Government agencies, banks or trusted brands.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why enforcement and public education remain essential.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But, Sir, I want to highlight one capability that I think deserves more recognition.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I recently visited the Anti-Scam Centre, and I was genuinely impressed by what I saw.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The public usually only sees the aftermath: reports filed, warnings issued, investigations underway.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But behind the scenes, the Anti-Scam Centre is doing time-sensitive operational work where minutes matter, coordinating information, tracing flows, engaging partners and acting quickly to disrupt and prevent further losses.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is relentless and it is easy for people to underestimate it precisely because when it works well, the story becomes "nothing happened".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But what "nothing happened" often means money was frozen in time, a scam network was disrupted, or more victims were prevented.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, Sir, I want to put on record my appreciation for the officers and partners involved.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their work is certainly underrated, and it is a key part of our national response.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, scams is a whole-of-society approach because scammers exploit multiple layers in our ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They use online platforms to reach victims at scale.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They use social engineering to push victims with messages.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They use mule accounts and laundering networks to move funds quickly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And they exploit gaps between systems, where responsibilities are unclear, or where speed of action is uneven.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why the private sector plays such a critical role not as an add-on, but as part of the frontline defence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, my questions to the Minister are these.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, fighting scams is a whole-of-society approach and the private sector plays an important role.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, a significant part of scam activity today is enabled or amplified online.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How can more be done to ensure that online platforms, such as Meta, Apple or Google, strengthen their anti-scam measures to better protect users?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the next step is to ensure that everyone in the ecosystem, especially those who control reach and virality, plays their part with the same seriousness and urgency.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, to counter the scourge of increasingly sophisticated scams, the implementation of targeted legislative mechanisms is essential.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Our laws must continue to provide authorities the power to effectively disrupt and disable criminal activity and infrastructure and create upstream defences to prevent or limit losses suffered by victims.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: But such progress can be reversed very quickly, however.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Scammers are constantly reinventing themselves and will adapt quickly.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: When public education raises awareness of certain tactics, they will simply pivot to trying something different.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Today, they may be capitalising on the popularity of Pokemon cards; tomorrow, they will ask their victims to buy and hand over gold bars, hoping that their ill-gotten gains will be harder to trace.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Scammers will increasingly use Generative AI to create ever more convincing phishing emails and deepfake voice or video calls for impersonation.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We need to strengthen our legislative levers to allow Singapore to act more effectively and decisively against scammers.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to hearing from MHA what systemic changes we will need to effect and how can we further strengthen our regulatory frameworks, to provide more tools to combat scams?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Alex Yeo, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is a positive development, and due credit must be given to the Police and, in particular, the officers of the Anti-Scam Command for their tireless efforts in combating scams to protect Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: On this note, I wish to highlight two areas for discussion.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Understandably, the topmost concern on the minds of scam victims, is whether they are able to recover their monies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is encouraging news, especially on the Anti-Scam Command's successful efforts in averting potential losses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: And yet, if we look at the amounts of monies recovered compared with the total amount lost, recovered monies represent only about 15% of the amounts lost.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: A large part of the reason for this is because of the transnational nature of scams.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Often, scam proceeds are transferred out of Singapore within minutes, if not, seconds, of the victim's transfer.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This makes it extremely challenging for the Police to trace and recover the monies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To this end, the establishment of FRONTIER+ in October 2024, a united front against transnational scams comprising 11 jurisdictions, is a landmark initiative that facilitates real-time intelligence sharing, joint operations and coordinated enforcement against transnational scams.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I therefore invite the Minister to share if there are plans to the expand the FRONTIER+ grouping, how successful do we think it has been in combating transnational scams and whether there are opportunities for Singapore to leverage on the grouping to recover more scam proceeds that have been transferred out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Second, notable steps have also been taken to enact or strengthen legislation to tackle scams, including the Online Criminal Harms Act (OCHA) Code of Practice, the Protection from Scams Act that was passed and operationalised last year, empowering the Police to issue Restriction Orders to banks to restrict the banking transactions of individuals at risk of transferring monies to scammers, the Facility Restriction Framework to tackle scam mules and the Criminal Law (Miscellaneous Amendment) Act which was passed in November 2025 which introduced caning for scam and scam-related offences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I also invite the Minister to share whether MHA feels that this is sufficient or if there are also plans to further strengthen legislative levers to tackle scams.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The recent 2025 statistics on the Drug Situation in Singapore released by the Central Narcotics Bureau raised a worrying trend of drug abuse among our youths.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In 2025, 28% of all drug abusers arrested were below 30 years of age.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The youngest drug abuser arrested in 2025 was just 12 years old.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The number of drug abusers below the age of 20 years old, increased year on year by 7%, while the number of new drug abusers arrested below 20 years old increased by 22%.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Notably, six in 10 new cannabis abusers arrested were below 30 years old.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We understand and appreciate deeply the damage and detrimental effects that drug abusers can cause, not only to themselves, but also to their family and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In recent years, there has been a worrying global shift in views and attitudes towards the use of drugs, such as cannabis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In 2020, the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs reclassified cannabis and cannabis resin under the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Thailand, a fellow ASEAN neighbour, became the first Asian country to decriminalise cannabis in 2022.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: How do we ensure that our youths are not influenced by global trends and attitudes towards drugs, like cannabis?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Recently, the Government had to also take urgent steps to address Kpods, which are e-vaporisers or vapes containing the psychoactive substance, etomidate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: A significant number of those who abuse Kpods are youths.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Anecdotally, I have sure many other Members of this House have as well, I have met many parents of teenagers and youths in the community who are extremely worried and concerned.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I invite the Minister to share with this House on the Government's plans to address global trends towards liberal drug approaches and how we can better effectively engage our youths on the dangers of drug abuse and substance abuse.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, recent tragedies, including the accident in Chinatown where a young child lost her life, are sobering reminders of how vulnerable our loved ones are on our roads.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Each incident is not just a statistic, but a family forever changed.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In that instance, the offender engaged in dangerous driving behaviour at a very high speed, including what was described as “blocking and braking” a motorcycle, before a collision occurred which resulted in the loss of life.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In particular, whether we should raise maximum sentences to allow our courts further flexibility to address different levels of culpability – from simple negligence at one end, to highly dangerous driving with a high risk of serious injury or death at the other.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Separately, enforcement and penalties are one aspect of ensuring safe roads, but they are not sufficient by themselves.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Ultimately, safer roads begin with a shared commitment – to look out for one another, and to remember that behind every road user is a family.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will the Minister consider further public education and training for road users in order to foster a culture of safety?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Scams continue to evolve at scale and sophistication, and they disproportionately affect those who are less digitally savvy, particularly our seniors.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We should continue to strengthen enforcement levers to act more effectively against scammers.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, we must also consider how best to balance deterrence with rehabilitation, especially for our youth offenders, those who have been drawn into such activity due to financial pressures or lack of awareness.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In Ayer Rajah, I had a particularly memorable case where a young graduate was looking for a job but fell to a job scam, ended up being a money mule and he was the sole breadwinner for a family of three, all of which were depending on him.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When he was charged, he fell further into financial difficulties.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must equip Singaporeans with the awareness and confidence to protect themselves – to recognise scam tactics, to exercise caution and to take personal responsibility in an increasingly digital world.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Behind every accident, every scam, is a family who suffers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the Home Team AI Movement was launched in 2024 with the vision of transforming our officers and how they safeguard Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry update on the AI products developed so far under this movement?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: How widely have these tools been deployed, and what measurable improvements have been observed in day-to-day operations?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: With the development of humanoid robots, capable of tackling high risk tasks such as firefighting and hazmat operations, how will these systems be integrated into frontline operations?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: What role will AI-enabled robotics play in augmenting our manpower given rising operational demands and manpower constraints across MHA?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: How is MHA reskilling our officers to prepare for these changes?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: With AI models such as Phoenix, built with partners Microsoft and Mistral AI, how does the Ministry ensure data security, model integrity, and responsible deployment across sensitive Home Team environments?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, these questions reflect the public’s interest in how AI will not replace officers, but empower them, enhance safety and strengthen trust in our security institutions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of these incidents involve our seniors, where distraction, medical conditions, or reduced mobility quickly turn an everyday activity into a serious safety risk.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Singapore becomes a super-aged society, preventing such incidents must form part of how we support seniors to be safe at home while giving a greater sense of peace of mind to their families and caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Japan, stoves are commonly equipped with built-in safety sensors that detect overheating and automatically shut off the gas before a fire can occur.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In South Korea, smart stove monitoring devices can alert users when appliances are left unattended and automatically cut off power to prevent accidents.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I would like to state that I am a founder of a company that deals with a low altitude economy business, which is basically large drones, or otherwise known as a flying car and, on the way, I am building firefighting drones, and also drones for oil spills.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, I think just on 19 February, a fire occurred at condominium in Kovan on the 14th floor.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: How can we apply and adapt these learning points to the Singapore context?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: On 25 February, CNA reported that hundreds of AI-generated online videos have been targeting Singapore and especially Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The wordings are all in complex Chinese or 繁体字.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: These are lots of fabrications about our leadership being under threat and spreading conspiracies.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Personally, I have also encountered many friends, business associates, voicing to me concerns on the impact on the business due to Prime Minister Wong's comments during the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, 19 November, last year.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I personally do not believe in all this stuff, so I view the video and find it to be actually quite neutral and factual.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the world is really facing a lot of geopolitical tension and contestations amongst major powers and of course, malicious actors will continue their attempts to coerce Singapore and also try to influence Singaporean to adopt policies that are advantageous to their foreign states' interest.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, social media come in all formats, podcasts – and we are talking about real time podcasts, short videos, TikTok or whatsoever.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: All are attempts to influence Singaporeans, which will impact the fabric of our society.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We have the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act, but the Government will not be able to identify all these online allegations and fake news.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The question is, how do we educate, inoculate, vaccinate, whatever terms that we want to use, to really equip our population, the various segments of our population – students, the community, the businesses – to really discern such activities.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I think critical thinking is very important, not just reading about it, but able to think for themselves, whether such news, such videos are attempts to influence us, and how can we have a series of awareness campaigns and events?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Really, I think it is a lot of education for our population to really have critical thinking about all these videos and decide for themselves whether these sources are trying to influence us.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you may take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The threat landscape today is increasingly complex and fraught with tension.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Around the world, domestic politics have become a target by external influence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is deeply plugged into a globalised world economy and economically.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Precisely because of this, we cannot afford to be naive about attempts by foreign actors to influence our domestic political discourse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore must never be put in a position where we are told, mandated or commanded to choose sides, or where external powers attempt to muscle us into adopting positions that do not serve our national interest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Decisions taken in this House, this House of Parliament must be guided by what benefits Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This House and MHA have been doing so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As parliamentarians, our duty is to assess, debate and vote on issues through that lens alone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We all have a collective responsibility to maintain such a mature posture when discussing and debating internal affairs and internal politics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore politics must remain the domain of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must therefore remain alert, resilient and united in safeguarding our political system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore must continue to send a clear signal that our politics is for Singaporeans to lead, manage and control.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not about shutting ourselves off from the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is about ensuring that while we remain open, engaged and principled internationally, our sovereignty, independence and democratic processes remain firmly protected and non-negotiable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most of all, we must be principled about discussing sensitive state topics, defence, internal security, race and religion in a sensible, cogent and respectable way in public discourse in Singapore and in this House.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In recent years, we have seen several jurisdictions liberalise their stance towards recreational drugs, particularly cannabis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More recently, some of these same jurisdictions are now attempting to reverse course.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thailand's U-turn is a case in point, but the critical question we must ask ourselves is this: while laws and policies can be reversed, can addiction be so easily undone?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can a permissive mindset towards recreational drugs be rolled back without long term and multi-generational consequences?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Once a society normalises recreational drug use, the social, health and crime-related costs do not simply disappear with a policy reversal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must also look out for new psychoactive substances and new drug concoctions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must remain firm against traffickers, resolute in enforcement and unwavering in our message to society, especially our youth, that there is no place for recreational drugs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our approach protects not just individuals but families and future generations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Staying firm today spares us deeper social costs tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's approach to drugs has always rested on moral clarity and deep resolve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We take a strong and uncompromising position against drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These laws must have teeth and rigour, because traffickers respond to cost-benefit calculations and deterrence must be real.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those who consume drugs and then become addicted are sometimes the innocent ones.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a society, we must do our best to help those who are genuinely intent on kicking the habit or undergoing mandatory drug rehabilitation to drop the addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires a scaffold after release, pathways into stable employment and support for reunification with families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Meaningful work, dignity and responsibility are critical catalysts for reintegration and for breaking the cycle of relapse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The reward and the road towards an addiction-free life is not easy, but it is worth a good try.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They too must take ownership of their own path to recovery.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But as a society, we should put in place schemes and funding to give them the best possible chance of kicking the drug addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this case, the Singapore Prison Service and the Drug Rehabilitation Centre and the CNB have key roles to play.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This reflects good policy-making, which requires what I call political ambidexterity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should not be straitjacketed into thinking in terms of left leaning policies or right leaning policies or be trapped by ideological labels.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What matters is whether a policy does right by people and addresses harm effectively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is nothing contradictory about taking a hard, uncompromising position against traffickers while adopting a more rehabilitative approach towards addicts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some may label rehabilitation as a left-leaning policy and tough enforcement against traffickers as a right-leaning policy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But that is not the correct lens, I humbly submit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The correct lens is whether the approach works, whether it is just and whether it protects society while giving individuals a chance to reform.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Strong laws against traffickers are necessary because trafficking is a rational, profit-driven crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Doing what is right often requires hard choices, balance and political nuance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, as with drugs, we should apply political ambidexterity in our legislative work in this House.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Before I start, I would like to thank Members for bringing up the drugs issue.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is an issue close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, the latest statistics from CNB give us reason to pause and reflect.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Cannabis use among youths also remains significant, with new abusers making up to 70% of cannabis arrests.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: They point to something deeper – a growing vulnerability among our young population.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond Singapore, the 2025 World Drug Report recorded a record 236 tonnes of methamphetamine seized in East and Southeast Asia in 2024.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Southeast Asia alone accounted for 94% of these seizures.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Taken together, this tells us we are facing two pressures at the same time: first, increasing exposure among our youths here at home; second, persistent and large-scale production and trafficking flows across the region.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's enforcement regime remains firm and respected.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is becoming more digital, more decentralised and more transnational.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister on four areas.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: First, given that one in two new abusers is now below 30 and the youngest arrested was only 12, does the Ministry intend to recalibrate its preventive outreach?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Should we be engaging children earlier, perhaps even before they enter secondary school?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Second, with methamphetamine dominating youth arrests, has the Ministry studied whether digital recruitment, especially through encrypted messaging platforms, is driving earlier exposure?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond taking down accounts and syndicates, what proactive digital countermeasures are we considering?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Third, at the regional level, given the record methamphetamine seizures and the continued synthetic drug flows, are we strengthening intelligence sharing and joint task force arrangements with key ASEAN partners?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Can we do more to disrupt supply chains further upstream instead of focusing at our borders?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, with female drug abusers rising from 15% to 19% of total arrests, should we also be examining whether gender-specific prevention and strategies are needed?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, this policy cut is not about weakening our firm stance on drugs.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: On the contrary, it reflects concern that the threat is evolving.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If one in two new abusers is under 30, and children as young as 12 are being drawn in, then prevention must move upstream – socially, digitally and regionally.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We must make sure our strategy stays ahead of the curve, rather than simply responding to it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, I would first like to start by thanking Members who spoke for their support of the Home Team's work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was the highest level of confidence in the Home Team over the past decade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we cannot for a moment rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The threat environment, as Members have pointed out, is constantly evolving, and the Home Team must keep pace.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are three areas of concern which we have been particularly monitoring.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore thrives by being open to information and welcoming to foreign talent, capital, goods and ideas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is commonplace for Singaporeans to consume information and perform transactions online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are our strengths, but it also means that we are more exposed to risks that originate from abroad.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Security threats such as radicalisation, foreign interference, scams and drugs are very much driven by external actors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These risks increase when the geopolitical environment becomes more fragmented and disorderly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We see one too many instances of careless and irresponsible behaviour, which have caused injuries and cost lives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fires involving active mobility devices (AMDs) accounted for almost 20% of fire-related injuries and more than 25% of fatalities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many of such fires stemmed from non-compliant devices and improper charging practices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to review our laws, policies and operations to ensure that they shape the behaviour and outcomes that society wants to see by enabling the authorities to be able to adequately deal with those who pose a danger to others through their behaviour.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Demands on Home Team officers have increased and will continue to increase in both volume and complexity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2025, traveller volumes through Singapore's checkpoints were up by 13% from 2019, before COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Calls for emergency medical services have increased by 35% from 2020, at the height of COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The number of scam cases have more than doubled from 2020 and the total amount lost to scams more than tripled.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Innovation and technology can help overcome our constraints to some extent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My colleagues and I will therefore speak on how the Home Team is addressing these challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Minister of State Faishal will cover the need to maintain our tough stance against drugs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will speak about technology adoption, including artificial intelligence (AI), as well as road safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Minister of State Goh Pei Ming will speak about our plans to fight scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the rest of this speech, I will speak about our efforts to address radicalisation, foreign interference and fire safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In November last year, a 17-year-old student detonated four explosive devices at a school mosque in Jakarta, injuring nearly 100 people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The perpetrator was said to have been inspired by far-right extremists.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A month later, during a gathering for the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at Bondi Beach in Sydney, two gunmen with anti-Semitic beliefs killed 15 people and injured many others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We cannot discount the possibility of similar attacks here.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Several of them had articulated an intention of carrying out attacks in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These were largely inspired by foreign conflicts; Islamist terrorist organisations, such as ISIS; and far-right extremism.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Internet has enabled such ideologies to proliferate and reach Singaporeans, often on their mobile screens.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Vikram Nair noted, youths are particularly susceptible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are digital natives and may find belonging and purpose in the virtual communities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the last two years, three 14-year-olds have been dealt with for terrorism-related activities, under the Internal Security Act (ISA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even video games have been exploited to promote extremism.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In a recent case, the individual posted pro-ISIS footage from online gaming platforms, such as Roblox and Gorebox, in which he role-played as a fighter for ISIS and recreated ISIS attacks and executions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we agree with Mr Nair on the need for early upstream intervention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are therefore intensifying our outreach efforts to inoculate youths against extremist ideologies and to sensitise the public to the telltale signs of radicalisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And these include interactive activities at SGSecure roadshows and other touchpoints, as well as digital engagement through our SGSecure Instagram, Facebook and TikTok accounts, places where you might typically find most of the youths.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To help youths and educators further recognise the signs of radicalisation, we organise workshops and forums with secondary schools, with junior colleges, madrasahs, the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), and we are extending such workshops to educators in all primary schools, as well as to student leaders and educators in all IHLs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But another important question is this: when an incident happens, how prepared are Singaporeans?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since its inception 10 years ago, SGSecure has made good progress in preparing the community with emergency preparedness skills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We now have about 250,000 Community Responders, who can be mobilised to respond and help one another when a crisis strikes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nonetheless, we still have some way to go when it comes to public vigilance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is therefore a need for Singaporeans to go beyond knowing what to do, to active vigilance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next week, we will launch a refreshed SGSecure campaign and series of roadshows that will shift the focus towards actions that Singaporeans can take before, during and after a terrorist attack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We hope that Singaporeans will respond to the call to action, stay vigilant and pick up skills and knowledge to help keep ourselves and fellow Singaporeans and those around us safe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In this landscape, as Dr Neo Kok Beng and Mr Christopher de Souza have pointed out, emotive and sensitive issues, such as race and religion, can be more easily exploited by foreign actors to deepen fault lines within our society and manipulate Singaporeans to be aligned with foreign interests, at the expense of our own interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: You must continue to strengthen our safeguards against foreign interference.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act (RHA), we will be designating race-based entities that are assessed to have higher potential of being vectors for malicious foreign interference.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the first instance, we will designate clan associations and business associations linked to the Chinese, Malay and Indian races.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These entities will need to disclose foreign donations and affiliations, and meet leadership composition requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also need to guard against evolving foreign interference tactics, which are becoming increasingly sophisticated and therefore harder to detect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One such example is inauthentic websites masquerading as credible sources, to launch hostile information campaigns (HICs).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2024, we identified 10 such websites, set up by foreign actors, that were masquerading as Singapore websites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They did so by using terms and images associated with Singapore to make it look and appear more local.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Most of the websites were associated with global networks of inauthentic news websites that had been reported by researchers to have conducted influence operations in other countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As there are currently no provisions in the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act (or FICA) to pre-emptively act against inauthentic websites, we relied on levers under the Broadcasting Act to geo-block these websites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was not as timely as it should be.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The overall fire incidence rate in Singapore remains stable and low by international standards, at about 2,000 incidents per year in the past five years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is in no small part due to our rigorous fire safety requirements and industry cooperation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the past three years, over 98% of the buildings which require a Fire Certificate (FC) have ensured that their fire protection systems remain reliable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Adequate safeguards, such as mandatory annual inspections, will still be retained under the three-year FC regime, to ensure that the buildings' fire protection systems remain functional.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Non-compliant buildings, however, will remain on a one-year FC regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is to incentivise good fire safety management and behaviour, whilst at the same time, lowering administrative and processing costs for compliant buildings' owners and occupiers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dr Neo has asked if there are any lessons to be learnt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Based on publicly available information, the Wang Fuk Court fire spread via the screening netting, which was mounted on the extensive bamboo scaffolding surrounding the building.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The spread was accelerated to catastrophic levels by flammable styrofoam panels that were used to cover the windows of the apartment units.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Singapore, we have stringent controls to mitigate the spread of fires.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At building and construction sites, bamboo scaffolds are not permitted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Fire Code stipulates that materials installed on the exterior of buildings must meet fire safety standards to prevent rapid spread of flames.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nevertheless, the authorities are thoroughly reviewing our scaffolds and netting safety regimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition to fire safety regulations, early fire detection is key.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It means more time to act, be it to extinguish fires or to evacuate safely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In that vein, Ms Rachel Ong spoke about technology-enabled devices like stove sensors, especially for seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government, indeed, recognises the importance of leveraging appropriate technology to enhance fire safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That is why, since June 2018, Home Fire Alarm Devices (HFADs) have been required for all new residential premises and existing premises undergoing fire safety works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: HFADs provide early warning of smoke or heat by sounding an alarm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is really a simple but effective solution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We strongly encourage all homeowners to install HFADs at the earliest opportunity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have various schemes to assist the elderly installing HFADs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And Members will know that my colleague, Minister for National Development, announced the extension of the Enhancement for Active Seniors programme to the private estates as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides HFADs, we will continue to explore other technologies for our elderly and incorporate them where appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, Sir, our regulatory frameworks also need to address emerging fire safety risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, whilst research has shown that fires in electric vehicles (EVs) are less likely than an internal combustion engine vehicles, EVs pose different risks when they catch fire and therefore require different management approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More information will be shared later this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can help SCDF responders more easily identify whether a vehicle is an EV and adopt specialised procedures during an incident.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes establishing a wider safety cordon to account for more intense flames.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And members of the public can also more readily identify that an affected vehicle is an EV and take precautions to stay away.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also dealing with fire safety risks from AMDs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Later this year, MOT plans to strengthen regulations on online sales and advertising of AMDs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The broader point here, Sir, is that powerful lithium-ion batteries are becoming more common.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today they are in many mobility devices and vehicles; tomorrow they may start appearing in more consumer goods.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to educate the public on how to properly use and maintain such batteries and how to respond when an incident occurs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, a high level of safety and security has enabled Singapore to thrive and succeed as a nation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Home Team will continue to anticipate and prepare for new and evolving challenges, and take strong and decisive action to protect and unite Singaporeans, in these turbulent times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, the global drug situation is getting more challenging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Drug use has also continued to rise globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The World Drug Report 2025 reported that 6% of the world's population, aged 15 to 64, used drugs in 2023.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Methamphetamine remains the most commonly abused drugs in Singapore, reflecting the worldwide trend.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Singapore's drug control strategy is anchored on tough laws and robust enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also invest in upstream preventive education and evidence-informed rehabilitation and reintegration programmes for abusers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This approach has proven effective and kept the drug situation here under control.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Jackson Lam asked whether we are strengthening intelligence-sharing and joint task force arrangements with ASEAN partners to disrupt drug supply further upstream.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB shares intelligence and extends support to foreign drug enforcement agencies to disrupt syndicates that attempt to traffic drugs into Singapore or exploit Singaporeans as couriers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Alex Yeo asked for an update on plans to address the rising trend of youth abusers and how we can effectively engage them on the dangers of drug abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2025, 3,208 drug abusers were arrested, a 1% increase from 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The number of young drug abusers is also on the rise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In the Health and Lifestyle Pulse Survey 2025 conducted by the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), around 1% of Singapore respondents said they had used a drug in the past year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: While this is lower than the 6% worldwide figure, we must continue to strengthen our preventive drug education efforts (PDE) to combat drug abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Inter-Ministry Committee on Drug Prevention for Youths started the Drug Victims Remembrance Day in 2024 – reminding everyone that drug abuse is not victimless, and its harms extend beyond the abusers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Last year, Remembrance Day focused on empowering young people as active participants and advocates against drugs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We garnered over 180,000 promises to stay drug-free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In schools, MOE supported CNB in developing age-appropriate materials for teachers to facilitate meaningful conversations about drug harms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Universities hosted spaces in their campus for reflection and dialogue about the harms of drugs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Planning for this year's Remembrance Day is underway.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The observance event will showcase stories from Singapore and overseas on how drugs have harmed lives, families and societies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will involve the wider drug-free community and community partners in our efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Besides Remembrance Day, CNB conducts DrugFreeSG campaigns to sustain amplification of the drug-free message.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Uninfluenced campaign was introduced in 2025, focusing on empowering youths to remain uninfluenced as they encounter multiple narratives about drugs, including misleading information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our first run featured an immersive theatre-cum-escape room event to pique youths' interest and provoke thought on evolving drug issues in a relatable way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We received encouraging feedback with participants who look forward to the next event.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2026, we will extend the Uninfluenced campaign through both online and physical engagements with tertiary students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will encourage them to reflect on the influences that shape their perceptions of drug abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Jackson Lam asked whether we should engage children before they enter secondary school.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB partners with MOE to integrate PDE content into the school curricula in educating students on the harms of drugs throughout their educational journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For primary schools, the focus is on general substance abuse and teaching impulse control skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Anti-Drug Ambassador Activity programme engages Primary 4 and 5 students through activity booklets with engaging storylines and interactive activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The 2025 National Drug Perception Survey found that attitudes towards drugs amongst youths have turned more conservative as more youths perceive that drug abuse is harmful. 87.7% held conservative views compared to 83.2% in 2023.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Attitudes towards drugs amongst adults remained staunchly conservative at 90.2%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will introduce a presumption clause for hair test results.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This means that if a controlled drug is found in a person's hair, they will be presumed to have abused it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This gives CNB a stronger tool for enforcement, since hair tests can detect abuse over a longer period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Jackson Lam asked if we have studied whether digital recruitment, especially among youths, is driving earlier exposure and whether we are considering proactive digital countermeasures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Health and Lifestyle Surveys include questions on why respondents tried drugs for the first time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The most common reasons cited for initiating drug abuse are due to curiosity, the belief that drugs will help them with their problems, and peer influence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Nonetheless, CNB takes a proactive approach by actively monitoring messaging apps and taking action against those who use such platforms to facilitate drug trafficking activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB also conducts operations on syndicates tapping on such platforms to sell drugs and works closely with the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) and courier companies to intercept drugs and drug-related paraphernalia sold online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Beyond education and enforcement, it is also important to rehabilitate drug abusers and support their reintegration into society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Last year, I spoke about the positive findings from the pilot under the "Supervision 2.0" regime, where hair tests are used to monitor CNB's supervisees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This cuts down the reporting frequencies from twice a week or twice a month depending on their risk profile, to once every three months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This reduction has allowed supervisees to go about their daily life with less disruption, helping them reintegrate better into society, while allowing CNB to have effective oversight of their rehabilitation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We are also seeing encouraging results on the rehabilitation efforts of Singapore Prison Service (SPS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We stay committed to supporting drug abusers in their rehabilitation journey through evidence-informed throughcare drug rehabilitation, and robust supervision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Drug abusers undergo differentiated drug rehabilitation, where programming pathways are customised based on the assessed risk of re-offending and severity of drug abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For repeat drug abusers who are of higher risk and require more intensive programmes, SPS has implemented a new Psychology-Based Correctional Programme (PCPs), that focuses on personal reflections, emotional processing and practical skills-building.
